clue.text: Woman suspecting husband of infidelity could become newly "de-married"

indicators.note: the letters of the two words could become something else when rearranged, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: A suspicious wife is ready to be newly unmarried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could become' shuffles NEWLY plus DEMARRIED. In Wilde's play Lady Windermere's Fan, the heroine suspects her husband of an affair with Mrs Erlynne.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's heroine wrongly believes her husband is unfaithful, which makes her the suspecting wife of the play.

clue.text: Album review? Try a back issue

indicators.note: to review is to look over again and rework, so the letters of album are rearranged

parts.note: a go is a try or attempt

explanation.surface: A music critic, after reviewing an album, is told to have a go at a back-catalogue release.
explanation.walkthrough: 'review' shuffles ALBUM into LUMBA. 'back issue' looks like an old magazine number but means a complaint of the back.
explanation.definitionFit: The ailment is pain in the lower spine, literally a problem with the back.

clue.text: Readers dig novel by Defoe, at first overlooked

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new or different, so these letters take a new order
only the opening letter of the novelist's name is taken

explanation.surface: Readers enjoy a Defoe novel that had initially been neglected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' sits right beside Defoe, tempting a reading as a book he wrote; here it is an adjective meaning new, signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ignored or passed over is to be overlooked, a direct synonym.

clue.text: "There's no possibility of being — without a little ill-nature" (The School For Scandal)

definitions.text: "There's no possibility of being — without a little ill-nature" (The School For Scandal)

parts.words: "There's no possibility of being — without a little ill-nature" (The School For Scandal)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Sheridan's comedy: the missing adjective describes clever, amusing talk

explanation.walkthrough: The line is spoken by Lady Sneerwell in Sheridan's The School for Scandal; the blank wants a word for sharply clever and amusing.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan's line says sparkling humour needs a touch of malice, so the gap takes a word for clever and humorous.

clue.text: Current time and place whence William Morris had news

parts.note: the present moment is now
here means this place

explanation.surface: A present-day location from which a Victorian designer received reports.
explanation.walkthrough: William Morris wrote the utopian novel News from Nowhere (1890).
explanation.definitionFit: Morris's utopian novel is titled News from Nowhere, so that is the source of his news.

clue.text: Group on the continent with inscription on grave above date for Roman or Greek tragedian

indicators.note: in a down clue the earlier pieces sit above the later one

parts.note: the European Union is a group of countries on the continent of Europe
RIP, rest in peace, is carved on headstones
the ides was a date in the Roman calendar, mid-month

explanation.surface: A European body puts an epitaph over a date, mourning an ancient dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' just joins wordplay to definition; 'Roman or Greek' looks like a choice of nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: He was one of the three great tragic dramatists of ancient Athens, alongside Aeschylus and Sophocles.

clue.text: Staff group that sponsored writing prize

definitions.meaning: to staff a post is to provide workers for it, a verb sense
the ... Group investment firm sponsored the Booker Prize from 2002 to 2019

explanation.definitionFit: To staff is to supply with workers, and the Man Group was the Booker's long-time sponsor.

clue.text: Philosopher regularly argues against hawk

indicators.note: every other letter of argues is taken, at regular intervals

parts.note: to hawk goods is to sell them

explanation.surface: A thinker keeps arguing against a bird of prey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of aRgUeS. 'hawk' looks like the bird or a war-monger but is the verb to peddle.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertrand Russell was a leading British logician and philosopher of the twentieth century.

clue.text: One of two sons abandons unsuitable literary family

indicators.note: one letter leaves the word it is in, so it is removed

parts.note: amiss means wrong or out of place
S is the abbreviation for son; the word for unsuitable has two of them

explanation.surface: A son walks out on an ill-suited family of writers.
explanation.walkthrough: The family of Kingsley and his son Martin, both novelists; the two S letters in the word for unsuitable are the two sons.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley and Martin, father and son, were both celebrated British novelists, making them a family of writers.

clue.text: Tasteless manner in which to decorate houses with marble

parts.note: a taw is a playing marble, especially the shooter

indicators.note: one word contains or houses the other

parts.note: to dress a shop window or street is to decorate it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A garish way to deck out homes with marble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'which to' merely links. 'houses' is a verb meaning contains, not dwellings, and a taw is the marble a child shoots with.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap, showy vulgarity is tastelessness, and the noun describes that manner.

clue.text: Character following Indian religion in audio book

indicators.note: the pieces are heard rather than read, as in an audiobook, so they are taken by sound

parts.note: air, meaning character or manner, comes after Jain, the Indian religion

explanation.surface: A character in an audiobook converts to an Indian faith.
explanation.walkthrough: JAIN plus AIR, said aloud, sounds like Charlotte Brontë's novel. 'following' sets the order.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte Brontë's 1847 novel is a classic book of English literature.

clue.text: I insert text copied from Russian writer, shortened by a third

indicators.note: the last three of nine letters, a third, are cut from the writer's name

parts.note: Boris Pasternak wrote Doctor Zhivago

explanation.surface: A plagiarist admits lifting passages from a Russian author, trimming them a bit.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks in the first person: someone who sticks in copied text could say 'I insert text copied'.
explanation.definitionFit: One who pastes is a person who puts in text that was copied, as with cut and paste.

clue.text: Weaver's woven sails, with sailor losing one

indicators.note: woven threads are interlaced and rearranged, so the letters of sails are reordered
a letter is dropped from the word for sailor

parts.note: a mariner is a sailor
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A weaver's sails are woven, with a sailor short of one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'woven' turns SAILS into SILAS; 'losing' drops I (one) from MARINER. 'Weaver's' is Weaver is.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's title character is a linen weaver in the village of Raveloe.

clue.text: A study of society project introduced by Carter

indicators.note: one piece comes after another that leads it in

parts.note: Howard Carter was the archaeologist who found Tutankhamun's tomb
to project is to send out or throw forward

explanation.surface: A sociological research project is introduced by a man named Carter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'project' is a verb, not a research scheme; 'introduced by' puts Carter's first name before it.
explanation.definitionFit: E M Forster's 1910 novel examines English class and society through three families.

clue.text: In Hades, demon avenges murder victim

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: In the underworld a fiend takes revenge for a killing.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across haDES DEMONAvenges. She is Othello's wife, smothered by him.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello kills his wife in Shakespeare's tragedy, so she is the play's murder victim.

clue.text: Charlie's 24 to her 50, getting love note

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
la is the sixth note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A big-brother figure gives her fifty, and she earns a love note.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 refers to the across answer BIG BROTHER: in Lauren Child's books Charlie is the big brother of his little sister.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lauren Child's picture books Charlie looks after his little sister, so he is her older male sibling.

clue.text: Poet's provided excerpt

indicators.note: an excerpt is a piece taken from within, here from inside one word

explanation.surface: A poet's work supplied an extract.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet sits inside prOVIDed; 'Poet's' is Poet is.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman author of the Metamorphoses is one of the great classical poets.

clue.text: From Rebecca's creator, this sensation scaling new heights?

definitions.meaning: Alfred Hitchcock directed the film Rebecca, so this is another film of his
a dizzy feeling felt when climbing to a great height

explanation.walkthrough: Hitchcock filmed Rebecca (1940) and also the 1958 thriller about a man afraid of heights; 'this' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Dizziness from height is the medical sense, and the same word titles a Hitchcock film.

clue.text: Priestess seething about time she was portrayed as ugly in fairytale

definitions.text: she was portrayed as ugly in fairytale

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round another one
seething means churning in turmoil, so the letters of priestess are stirred up

explanation.surface: A furious priestess, around this time, played a nasty part in a fairy story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seething' shuffles PRIESTESS into STEPSISER and 'about' puts T inside. Cinderella's two sisters are the ugly ones of pantomime.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinderella's stepfamily includes two cruel girls, traditionally played as the Ugly Sisters.

clue.text: Butler's satire sending up 4 (approximately)

indicators.note: the reversal is only approximate, so two of its letters are rearranged
in a down clue sending a word up reads it from bottom to top, reversing it

parts.note: refers to the answer to clue 4, meaning no place

explanation.surface: Samuel Butler's satire mocks the answer to clue 4, roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sending up' reverses NOWHERE to EREHWON, and '(approximately)' swaps H and W. 'sending up' also means mocking, apt for satire.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Butler's 1872 novel is a satirical utopia set in an imaginary country.

clue.text: Card game player gets by as quasi-professional poet

parts.note: Ender plays the war game in Ender's Game by Orson Scott Card
taken as written

explanation.surface: A card player gets by as a semi-pro versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Card' is the novelist Orson Scott Card, not playing cards. Anthony Burgess's comic novels follow a poet of that name who writes on the lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: Burgess's Mr Enderby is a poet who writes seriously but lives on very little, an amateur in professional dress.

clue.text: Investigator of Atkinson's cheese sandwiches overdose

indicators.note: the cheese surrounds another piece, as bread does a filling

parts.note: brie is a soft French cheese

explanation.surface: A detective finds cheese sandwiches laced with too much of a drug.
explanation.walkthrough: Kate Atkinson's detective novels feature Jackson Brodie; 'sandwiches' is a verb meaning encloses.
explanation.definitionFit: Kate Atkinson writes crime novels starring private investigator Jackson Brodie.

clue.text: "Dame Beryl Bainbridge, actress and writer's latest pieces" edited into "Beryl pieces"

indicators.note: editing reworks the material into a new arrangement
the latest piece of each word is its final letter

explanation.surface: An editor turns a tribute to a dame, actress and novelist into something about gems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'latest pieces' takes the last letters L, E, S, R; 'edited into' shuffles them with DAME. Beryl is a mineral of which green gems are one variety.
explanation.definitionFit: These green gemstones are a variety of the mineral beryl, so pieces of beryl.

clue.text: Retrospectively abridged Lorna Doone finally put on record

indicators.note: looking back, so the letters are read in reverse order
abridged means shortened, so the final letter is cut
the last letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A shortened Lorna Doone is looked back on before being filed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abridged' cuts Lorna to LORN, 'finally' adds E from Doone, and 'Retrospectively' turns LORNE round.
explanation.definitionFit: To register someone officially is to enter their name on a list or record.

clue.text: Huge fuss about introduction of right-wing state's surveillance operation

parts.note: big means huge

indicators.note: the word for fuss goes round another letter

parts.note: bother is fuss or trouble

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A huge row breaks out over a right-wing government's spying programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'introduction of' takes R from right-wing; 'about' puts it inside BOTHER. In Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four the watching leader is this figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's all-seeing figurehead has become the name for intrusive state surveillance.

clue.text: Offer book proposal that's half-finished

indicators.note: only half the word is completed, so its last half is dropped

parts.note: an idea is a proposal or suggestion

explanation.surface: A publisher's bid for a book proposal only half written.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-finished' cuts IDEA to ID; 'that's' links. 'book proposal' reads as one publishing term.
explanation.definitionFit: A bid is an offer, as at an auction or in a takeover.

clue.text: Obsessive fan's buried in A Scanner Darkly

indicators.note: the letters lie buried within the words of the title

explanation.surface: A devotee is engrossed in a Philip K Dick novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across scanNER Darkly; 'fan's' is fan is.
explanation.definitionFit: A geek obsessed with a niche subject, such as science fiction, is called this.

clue.text: Burnett's boy considered Little Mix or Nelly Furtado

indicators.note: to mix is to jumble, so the following letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A children's-book hero is compared with a girl band or a pop singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mix' shuffles OR NELLY FURTADO. Little Mix is a British girl group; Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote Little Lord Fauntleroy.
explanation.definitionFit: Burnett's novel is titled Little Lord Fauntleroy, so its boy hero is known by that phrase.
